items.title: Bring insights and action together with Fabric Apps in Org apps
items.excerpt: Business users move from understanding what happened, to investigating why, to acting. Microsoft Fabric can bring that journey together. Fabric Apps provide purpose-built, data-driven experiences when users need more than a report. Org apps distribute them alongside Power BI reports and other supported Fabric content in a curated destination. Move from insight to action in one destination Power BI reports help users monitor performance, explore trends, and understand what’s happening in the business. Many insights, however, lead to a next step: submitting a request, updating a plan, investigating an exception, assigning an owner, or tracking a resolution. A Fabric App provides the custom interface and workflow for that next step. Including it in an org app places action beside the reports and operational content that provide context. Users enter one destination organized around their role, review the insight, open the Fabric App, and act. items.title: More ways to use scalar UDFs in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview)
items.excerpt: Scalar user-defined functions (UDFs) let data teams define a business rule once and reuse it across workloads in both Warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint in Microsoft Fabric. This helps teams maintain consistent logic without duplicating it across queries. Some business rules require more than a single expression. They use procedural logic such as conditional branches, multiple RETURN statements, or WHILE loops. Expression Block inlining compiles and executes this logic in a distributed manner, helping reusable functions scale across analytical workloads. Building on that foundation, this update brings several improvements: More natural loop control and broader query-shape support. Automatic adoption of newly supported capabilities by existing functions, without recreating or altering them. Inlineability validation for new or changed functions, with diagnostics that explain any gaps and an explicit WITH INLINE = AUTO override when a non-inlineable function is acceptable. Express loop intent with BREAK and CONTINUE Loops often need to skip the rest of the current iteration or stop processing entirely. items.title: On-premises data gateway October 2026 release
items.excerpt: The October 2026 release of the on-premises data gateway (version 3000.338) continues our commitment to secure, reliable and accessible connectivity between on-premises data sources and Microsoft Fabric services. This release focuses on accessibility, configuration reliability, and troubleshooting. It makes the installer and configurator more inclusive, keeps your Power Query settings intact during connection tests, and makes service-start failures easier to diagnose. It also brings compatibility updates for the October 2026 release of Power BI Desktop, so queries run the same way in Power BI Desktop and in cloud refreshes. items.title: Announcing workspace monitoring integration for Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview)
items.excerpt: With Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse integration with workspace monitoring (Preview), you can analyze completed warehouse query activity across an entire workspace from the monitoring Eventhouse and KQL database, helping you find failed or slow queries and quickly identify the warehouse that needs attention. See warehouse activity across your workspace Monitoring multiple warehouses is difficult when query activity is spread across separate tools and experiences. Workspace monitoring brings completed warehouse execution events into the WarehouseExecutions table, where administrators and operators can review activity across the workspace from a single monitoring database. The integration supports warehouses, SQL analytics endpoints, and warehouse snapshots. It captures completed, user-initiated queries that use distributed execution and records details such as duration, status, result codes, and CPU time. With this information in one place, you can spot failures or performance issues and focus your investigation on the affected warehouse and query. items.title: Introducing the data engineering agent for Fabric (Project Osmos)
items.excerpt: AI coding assistants are excellent at turning natural-language transformation instructions into code. For data engineers, the harder question is whether that code produces results they can trust. You can describe transformation logic in natural language, and an AI coding assistant will happily generate hundreds of lines of Spark code. Impressive. But a Spark job can execute successfully and still produce completely wrong results. The logic may work for a subset of the data but fail when run against the full dataset. The pipeline's logic and validation checks may not account for future changes to the data or schema. Incremental loads can cause duplicates. Revenue numbers might look perfectly reasonable until someone reconciles them against the source. Anyone who's spent time working with real-world enterprise data knows that automating data engineering with AI comes with a unique set of challenges. Data engineering involves more than code: it requires working with large datasets and retaining context about their schemas, relationships, and business rules over time.
